source_read: PDF (version of record), Br J Clin Pharmacol 1997;44:521-526, all six pages read (pp. 521-526, including acknowledgement and references). Text extracted with pdftotext -layout into my own folder; every number checked on pages rendered at 150 dpi; Table 1 (p. 524) checked on the rendered page; Figure 1 (p. 523) read at 300 and 600 dpi, values read from it labelled approximate.

claims.overstatement: None material. 'Reduced' is causal, but the within-person randomized crossover with an objective outcome supports it for these conditions, and the claim states the limits (one small dose, young men only, no impairment measure, no printed meal-versus-fasting test, mechanism not measured, composition question underpowered). Two small precision points: (1) time to peak is counted from the start of alcohol dosing (Methods, p. 522), so 'peak came 30 to 90 minutes after drinking' should read 'after the start of drinking' (drinking took up to 15 min); (2) the protein-rich breakfast had 9.0 and 9.6 in 100 more energy than the carbohydrate- and fat-rich ones, i.e. about 9 to 10 in 100.
claims.note: Every number from this source checked on the rendered pages (abstract p. 521; Methods p. 522; Results p. 523; Table 1 p. 524). Editors' calculations recomputed and reproduced: meal peaks 43.2, 53.9 and 57.5 in 100 of the fasting peak (protein-, fat-, carbohydrate-rich); meal AUCs 39.6, 55.0 and 50.4 in 100 of the fasting AUC; protein-rich peak 19.9 and 24.9 in 100 lower than the fat- and carbohydrate-rich peaks, AUC 28.1 and 21.6 in 100 lower. With the five-condition residual SD (5.1 mg/dl; 465.2 mg/dl.min) and SE of a within-person difference = s_res x sqrt(2/9) (2.40 mg/dl; 219.3 mg/dl.min), the meal-fasting differences are 5.9, 5.4 and 7.3 SE for peaks and 6.6, 7.3 and 8.8 SE for AUCs: about 5 to 9, as stated (assumes sphericity). CVs recomputed from means and SDs match Table 1 except the intravenous AUC (446/4786 = 9.3%, printed 10%), which the claim does not use. Two qualifiers the claim could carry: (a) Figure 1f suggests the fed-versus-fasting difference in time to reach zero is under an hour (meal mean curves near zero at about 190-200 min; the fasting mean is about 6 mg/dl at its last plotted point, about 190 min, and only a dashed extension reaches zero at about 235 min), smaller than the authors' 1 to 2 h, which the claim already treats as not measured; (b) the authors attribute the slow fasting elimination rate (about 10 against an often-cited 15 mg/dl per hour) to the 10-12 h fast itself (p. 524), so the fasting comparator may itself have slowed elimination. The authors' unpublished observation that the food effect was larger the shorter the interval between meal and drink (p. 525) is not data from this study; the claim's 'did not test ... longer gaps' is correct.

anchors.locator: Abstract > Methods (p. 521); Methods > Subjects and conditions, 1st paragraph (begins p. 521, continues p. 522)
anchors.extracted: Nine healthy men, all non-smokers, mean age 24.6 years (SD 4.8), body weight 75.8 kg (SD 9.0), height 183 cm (SD 4.6), paid volunteers, University Hospital, Linkoping, Sweden. Ethanol 0.30 g/kg body weight on five occasions in a randomized crossover: three times within 15 min of a standardized breakfast of similar volume and energy but different fat, carbohydrate and protein content, once after an overnight fast, once by intravenous infusion over 30 min.

anchors.locator: Methods > Subjects and conditions, 1st and 2nd paragraphs
anchors.extracted: At least 7 days between sessions (intervals not the same for every man); randomized crossover order (method not described). Ethanol (96% v/v) diluted with orange juice to a 20% v/v drink finished within exactly 15 min; intravenous dose 6% w/v in saline at a constant rate over 30 min. Breakfasts of ordinary Swedish breakfast foods relatively high in fat (55% of energy), protein (31%) or carbohydrate (86%), about 3000 kJ (700 kcal), eaten in 15 min, drink taken a few minutes later; fasting condition after an overnight (10 h) fast. Study conditions only.

Mean +/- SD, n = 9 per condition. Energy: high-fat 2908 kJ (fat 55%, CHO 33%, protein 12%), high-CHO 2924 kJ (9%, 86%, 6%), high-protein 3188 kJ (24%, 45%, 31%). Peak BAC mg/dl (CV%): 16.6 +/- 4.0 (24%), 17.7 +/- 7.1 (40%), 13.3 +/- 4.0 (30%); p.o. fasting 30.8 +/- 4.3 (14%); i.v. 54.3 +/- 6.4 (12%). AUC 0-210 min, mg/dl.min (CV%): 1767 +/- 549 (31%), 1619 +/- 760 (47%), 1270 +/- 406 (32%), 3210 +/- 527 (16%), 4786 +/- 446 (10%). tmax ranges: 30-90, 30-90, 30-60, 30-60 and 30 min. Three-meal ANOVA: DF printed 2 and 17, F = 2.22 (peak) and 2.42 (AUC), residual SD 4.4 and 492.5, power 0.221 and 0.251. Five-condition ANOVA: DF 4 and 32, F = 98.7 and 88.9, residual SD 5.1 and 465.2, power 1.0.

anchors.locator: Results, 2nd paragraph (begins p. 522; F values and power at top of left column, p. 523)
anchors.extracted: Differences across the five conditions highly significant (F = 98.7 for peak BAC, F = 88.9 for AUC, P < 0.001; post hoc power 1.0). The three meals did not differ significantly (F = 2.22 and 2.42, P > 0.05); the authors ask for caution because post hoc power was 0.22 (peak) and 0.25 (AUC). No test of any meal against fasting is printed, although the Methods (p. 522) say paired t-tests were used when two treatments were compared.

Between-person variability (CV%) in peak BAC and AUC greatest after food. Fasting and intravenous conditions only: disappearance rate 10.3 +/- 1.8 (fasting) against 9.8 +/- 1.2 mg/dl per hour (i.v.), 95% CI of the difference -2.27 to 1.25; Co 37 +/- 4.9 against 40 +/- 3.9 mg/dl, CI -1.6 to 7.0; Vd 0.81 +/- 0.11 against 0.75 +/- 0.08 l/kg, CI -0.154 to 0.033.

anchors.locator: Methods > Pharmacokinetics of ethanol, 1st and 2nd paragraphs
anchors.extracted: Peak BAC and time to peak noted from the start of alcohol dosing; AUC by the linear trapezoidal method from 0 to 210 min; bioavailability cannot be computed as an AUC ratio because ethanol elimination is saturable, so AUC compares conditions at the same dose. After food, individual peaks were often below 10-15 mg/dl, curves highly variable, sometimes with a secondary peak several hours after drinking ended, so curves could not be fitted and no elimination rate was estimated for the fed conditions.

Authors: drinking 0.30 g/kg after a meal, whatever its composition, caused a pronounced lowering of peak BAC and a marked decrease in AUC compared with an empty stomach or i.v. delivery; disposal faster because the time to eliminate ethanol from blood was 1-2 h shorter, citing Figure 1 (no measured value; same statement in Abstract > Results, p. 521). Figure 1f, mean curves read at 600 dpi (approximate): meal curves near zero at about 190-200 min; fasting mean about 6 mg/dl at its last plotted point (about 190 min), dashed extension reaching zero at about 235 min; i.v. mean about 1.5 mg/dl at 300 min.

Two proposed explanations, neither measured in this study: hepatic first-pass metabolism when slow, variable gastric emptying keeps portal ethanol low (Michaelis-Menten kinetics; Km of class I ADH 1-10 mg/dl in vitro, in vivo Km 6.7 and Vmax 18.1 mg/dl cited from other work), or a two-pool model with part of the dose bound to the meal and released slowly; one man showed a secondary peak about 2 h after drinking ended.

Disappearance rate in the fasting and i.v. conditions (about 10 mg/dl per hour) lower than the 15 mg/dl per hour often cited for moderate drinkers; the authors attribute this to 10-12 h of food deprivation, citing other work. No major significance of the macronutrients; the protein-rich meal tended to give lower BAC profiles, not significantly; the CHO-rich meal showed the most between-person variation.

anchors.locator: Discussion, 5th paragraph (continued from p. 524) to 7th paragraph; acknowledgement
anchors.extracted: Time-response studies of food and BAC not reported; the authors noted a more pronounced influence the shorter the time between meal and drink, as unpublished work (no data in this paper). Conclusion: food in the stomach before drinking lowers peak BAC and AUC considerably against an empty stomach or i.v. delivery; meal composition judged not so important. Funding in part from the Swedish National Board of Forensic Medicine and the Forensic Science Centre, Linkoping.

key_findings.correction: Checked on pp. 521-522: nine non-smoking men, mean age 24.6 (SD 4.8), 75.8 kg (SD 9.0); 0.30 g/kg in five sessions at least 7 days apart, randomized crossover. The 10-hour overnight fast is in the 2nd paragraph (p. 522), as the locator says.
2908, 2924 and 3188 kJ and the energy shares match Table 1 (p. 524); meals eaten in 15 min, drink a few minutes later and finished within exactly 15 min (p. 522).
All five means and SDs match the abstract (p. 521) and Table 1 (p. 524).
Values match; editors' calculation reproduced (meal peaks 43.2-57.5% and meal AUCs 39.6-55.0% of the fasting values).
F = 98.7 and 88.9 with DF 4 and 32 (Table 1), P < 0.001 and power 1.0 (p. 523; Table 1 footnote 3); no meal-versus-fasting test printed.
F = 2.22 and 2.42, P > 0.05; power 0.22 and 0.25 in the text (p. 523), 0.221 and 0.251 in Table 1 footnotes 1-2 (p. 524); the protein-rich tendency is in Discussion, 5th paragraph (p. 524).

Ranges match the tmax column. For clarity, tmax is counted from the start of alcohol dosing (Methods > Pharmacokinetics of ethanol, 1st paragraph, p. 522), not from the meal; the wording 'after the fat-rich ... meals' names the condition.
CVs match Results, 3rd paragraph (p. 523) and Table 1 (p. 524); recomputed from means and SDs they agree except the i.v. AUC (9.3%, printed 10%), already listed as a reporting issue.
All values and intervals match Results, 3rd paragraph (p. 523).

p. 522, Pharmacokinetics of ethanol, 2nd paragraph: individual peaks often below 10-15 mg/dl; a secondary peak sometimes several hours after the end of drinking; curves could not be fitted for the fed conditions.

My own 600-dpi reading of Figure 1f agrees: meal curves near zero at about 190-200 min; fasting mean about 6 mg/dl at its last point (about 190 min) with a dashed extension to zero at about 235 min; i.v. mean about 1.5 mg/dl at 300 min. The fed-fasting difference in time to zero is under an hour and rests partly on the dashed extension.
Content confirmed. Location detail: the 2nd Discussion paragraph begins on p. 523 (right column) and continues on p. 524; the first-pass explanation is also in Abstract > Conclusions (p. 521).
p. 524, Discussion, 4th paragraph: about 10 against 15 mg/dl per hour; attributed to 10-12 h of food deprivation (ref 27).

reporting_issues.note: Table 1 prints DF = 2 and 17 for the three-meal ANOVA; 2 and 16 are expected for 9 men in 3 conditions (the five-condition 4 and 32 is consistent). Recomputed: F = 2.22 gives P = 0.141 with (2, 16) and 0.139 with (2, 17); F = 2.42 gives 0.121 and 0.119.

Confirmed at 600 dpi: individual curves in panels a-d end at about 190 min; in panel f the fasting and meal means have points about every 10 min from 150 to 190 min and the i.v. mean every 10 min from about 210 to 300 min. The i.v. mean also has points at about 40 and 50 min where the stated schedule has 45 min.

Each condition was given once per man, so repeatability within a person under the same condition was not measured; the authors may mean differences between one man's three meal sessions, which the paper does not quantify.
3188/2908 = 1.096 and 3188/2924 = 1.090; meal volume or weight is not reported anywhere; the protein-rich meal took 45% of its energy from carbohydrate and 31% from protein (Table 1, p. 524).

risk_of_bias.note: RoB 2 fits a randomized crossover with an objective outcome. Some concerns overall is right: the randomization method is not described, there is no protocol, and the paired comparisons the Methods announce are not reported; carryover is implausible with at least 7 days between single small doses.

interpretation_gap.note: Minor: the central result (lower peak and AUC after food at this dose) is reported accurately; the gaps are the composition statement resting on a test with power about 0.2, the unmeasured mechanisms and the unquantified 1-2 h elimination statement, all of which the card records.
